y-m-27-03.title: Make two-digit even numbers with five cards
y-m-27-03.topic: Number of cases: make numbers under conditions (0 no fit be in tens place; no use one card twice)
y-m-27-03.goal: Make numbers wey meet conditions yourself (0 no fit be tens digit; each card use only once), and find and explain where counting methods under these conditions fit go wrong.
y-m-27-03.material: There are 5 cards, one each with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Choose 2 different cards and arrange dem to make two-digit whole number (first card na tens digit, next na ones digit). 0 no fit be tens digit (for example, 03 no be two-digit whole number). Each card fit use only once (for example, no fit make 22).
y-m-27-03.thinking.0: Make examples wey meet the conditions
y-m-27-03.prereq.0: Tens and ones digits of a two-digit whole number
y-m-27-03.prereq.1: Experience counting options when several choices follow one another
y-m-27-03.s.s1.prompt: How many two-digit whole numbers fit you make with these cards altogether?
y-m-27-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write all cards wey fit go for tens digit.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.hint.1: After choosing one tens card, count how many remaining cards fit go for ones digit.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.a: Na calculation wey count first card as 5 choices out of 5. Think if you also count cases where 0 go tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.b: Na calculation wey check how many choices tens and ones each get, and if dem affect each other.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.c: You count cases where same card use twice too. Check if you fit make 22 or 44.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.d: E look like you count too few ones-digit choices. After choose tens digit, count the remaining cards.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.explain: For tens digit, 4 cards fit come: 1, 2, 3, 4; leave out 0. For ones digit, the other 4 cards fit come, including 0 but leave the tens card, so 4×4=16.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different two-digit even whole numbers under the same conditions. (Enter the numbers you make.)
y-m-27-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide which card must go in ones place for the number to be even.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing ones card, check by crossing out each card to see which ones fit go for tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.var.n: The two-digit even number you make
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The cards na 0 to 4, so the number must be from 10 to 44.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Tens card no fit be 0, and choose only from 0 to 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Ones place na digit on a card.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Ones digit too must be from 0 to 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c4: You no fit use the same card for tens and ones digits.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c5: E no even. For even number, which digit must ones place get?
y-m-27-03.s.s2.explain: If ones digit na 0, tens digit fit be 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 numbers); if ones na 2, tens fit be 1, 3, 4 (3 numbers); if ones na 4, tens fit be 1, 2, 3 (3 numbers). So 10 even numbers dey: 10, 12, 14, 20, 24, 30, 32, 34, 40, 42.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.prompt: Seojin calculate, “Even numbers na 4 tens choices × 3 ones choices (0, 2, 4)=12.” Why this calculation wrong? Choose the best reason.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.hint.0: List all 12 and compare dem with the 10 you check in s2.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.hint.1: When ones card na 2, list the cards wey fit go for tens.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.a: This na case where we suppose add, no multiply
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.a: This na situation where we choose tens digit first then ones, so multiplication correct. Check what numbers dey inside the multiplied result.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.b: It no count case where 0 go tens place
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.b: The 4 tens choices already count only 1 to 4. Write the 12 numbers yourself and look at dem.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.c: You need find more possible even ones digits apart from 0, 2, 4
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.c: Among cards 0 to 4, the only even digits na 0, 2, 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.d: Numbers using same card twice, like 22 and 44, dey mixed in the 12
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.d: If you write the 12 numbers counted by multiplication, you go see numbers wey no fit make.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.explain: The 4 tens choices times 3 ones choices include numbers with same card twice, like 22 and 44. Remove those 2 from 12 and 10 correct. Since tens choices differ (4, 3, 3) depending on ones card, another method na split by ones digit and count.

y-m-27-04.prereq.0: Experience counting options when several choices follow one another
y-m-27-04.title: Does the calculation “20 choices” fit every kind of selection?
y-m-27-04.topic: Number of cases: selections where order matter and where e no matter
y-m-27-04.goal: Find why same calculation give different result when selected people get different roles and when roles no matter; correct the count by checking how many times one combination counted.
y-m-27-04.material:
Choose 2 duties among 5 choir members (가온, 나리, 다솜, 라온, 마루).
(A) Choose 1 president and 1 vice president. One person no fit take both roles.
(B) Choose 2 people for stage-cleaning duty. Both do the same work.
Eunu solve both as “5×4=20 ways”. Eunu solution here:
y-m-27-04.thinking.2: Find and correct how many times something was counted repeatedly
y-m-27-04.prereq.1: Experience listing all cases using symbols instead of names
y-m-27-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Eunu solution wey hard to believe.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.hint.0: For (A) and (B), work out if swapping the two chosen people make a difference or still same.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.hint.1: Shorten names to 가, 나, 다, 라, 마 and check if (가, 나) and (나, 가) same case for (A) and (B).
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.1: After choosing president, the other 4 fit be vice president. So (A) get 5×4=20 ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.2: For (B) too, first person get 5 choices, then second get 4 choices.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.3: So (B) too get 5×4=20 ways, and (A) and (B) get same number of ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 correct. President and vice president different roles, so (가온 president, 나리 vice president) and (나리 president, 가온 vice president) different cases, and 20 ways correct. The problem start at line 3. For (B), both roles same, so (가온, 나리) and (나리, 가온) na same duty pair, but 5×4 count both separately, counting one pair twice. So line 4 conclusion “(A) and (B) same” wrong too.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.prompt: How many ways altogether to choose 2 people for stage-cleaning duty in (B)?
y-m-27-04.s.s2.hint.0: Shorten names to symbols and list pairs in order, start with those containing 가.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many times one pair (like 가온 and 나리) dey inside the 20 ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.a: Na value counted as 5×4. Check if you count cases where both people swap order separately.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.b: E look like value for choosing only one person. List cases where 2 people choose yourself.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.c: Na calculation wey count same 2 people as one even when only order change.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.d: Na value wey even count choosing the same person twice. Both 2 duty people must be different.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.explain: 5×4=20 count pairs like (가온, 나리) and (나리, 가온) separately, only because order change. Each duty pair count twice, so 20÷2=10 ways. If you list directly as 가나, 가다, 가라, 가마, 나다, 나라, 나마, 다라, 다마, 라마, also 10.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.prompt: If (B) change to “3 duty people”, how many ways fit you choose 3 among the 5? (Roles same.)
y-m-27-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write all orders wey 3 people 가, 나, 다 fit stand in, and count the orders.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check if you get same answer by splitting cases according to who no choose.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.a: Na value wey come from checking how many times same 3 people count. You get same value by looking at people wey no choose.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.b: Na value wey stop after 5×4×3. Check if same 3 people counted several times when only order change.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.c: Na value divided by only 2 like the 2-person case. Work out how many orders 3 people fit line up.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.d: Na value wey use 5×4 only. E miss choosing the third person.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.explain: 5×4×3=60 count the order of choosing 3 people too. Same 3 people fit line up 3×2×1=6 ways, so every combination count 6 times. 60÷6=10 ways. Choosing 3 of 5 same as choosing the 2 we no choose, so e also equal the 10 ways to choose 2.

y-m-27-06.title: A marble question with two different answers
y-m-27-06.topic: Calculate probability: difference between drawing with replacement and without replacement
y-m-27-06.goal: Find say missing condition (whether put marble back) decide answer; compare probability for both conditions, and work out how difference change when number of marbles get large.
y-m-27-06.material:
Bag get 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. Marbles only differ by color and same shape and size, so with eyes closed you no fit know which one come out. Draw one marble at a time, twice, and check colors.
Question: “What be chance both marbles drawn same color?”
Eunseo answer 13/25 and Doyun answer 2/5. Neither make calculation mistake under their own method. But question no talk if marble go back inside bag after drawing.
y-m-27-06.thinking.2: Estimate change when numbers become large
y-m-27-06.prereq.0: Experience finding chance of something wey happen several times in a row
y-m-27-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write how many marbles Eunseo and Doyun each assume dey in bag for second draw.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find where the denominators dem use, 5 and 4, become different.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.a: Only Eunseo correct. Putting marble back na the normal rule
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.a: Question no talk about putting am back. Think if you add that assumption yourself by calling it normal.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.b: Only Doyun correct. Obviously the marble wey draw stay outside
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.b: Question no talk say no put am back either. Think if you assume that as obvious.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.c: Both wrong. Two colors dey, so same-color probability na 1/2
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.c: Red marbles plenty, so both colors no appear equally often. Look at marble count, no be color count.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.d: We no fit decide without knowing if marble put back
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.d: You notice say missing condition decide answer. Good to check value under both conditions.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.explain: If you put am back, second draw still get 3 red and 2 blue, so (3/5)×(3/5)+(2/5)×(2/5)=13/25. If you no put am back, 4 remain, so (3/5)×(2/4)+(2/5)×(1/4)=2/5. Both values different, so without knowing if e put back, we no fit decide.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.prompt: What condition each answer need so e go be correct?
y-m-27-06.s.s2.hint.0: Compare denominators for second probability in both expressions.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check if second probability numerators (red count, blue count) depend on first result.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.a: Eunseo put am back; Doyun no put am back
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.a: Each one judge based on whether marble count for second draw na 5 or 4.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.b: Eunseo no put am back; Doyun put am back
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.b: Use Eunseo expression, denominator 5, to check how many marbles remain at second draw.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.c: Both put am back; only calculation method different
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.c: If you put am back, denominator still 5 for second draw. Check Doyun denominator.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.d: Neither put am back; only calculation method different
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.d: If you no put am back, denominator for second draw na 4. Check Eunseo expression.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.explain: Eunseo expression (3/5)×(3/5)+(2/5)×(2/5) draw second marble from 5 again, so na replacement case. Doyun expression (3/5)×(2/4)+(2/5)×(1/4) draw second from 4, so na without replacement.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.prompt: If marbles increase to 30 red and 20 blue (same 3:2 ratio) and you compare both conditions, how the difference between probabilities compare with the start (3 red, 2 blue)?
y-m-27-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the denominator for probability of second draw without replacement, for original and new case.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate both condition probabilities as decimals and compare them with the earlier difference.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.a: The gap bigger pass the first one
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.a: Compare how much the marbles left after taking one out decrease when total number of marbles large.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.b: E exactly the same as first gap
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.b: Even if ratio same, number of marbles left after taking one out different. Compare denominator 5 and 4 with 50 and 49.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.c: E become so small e nearly disappear
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.c: You notice when many marbles dey, taking one out hardly change wetin remain.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.d: The case where we no put am back actually get bigger
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.d: Compare with the original value 2/5 being smaller than 13/25. Write expression and calculate to check.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.explain: If we put am back, (30/50)²+(20/50)²=13/25=0.52; without replacement, (30/50)(29/49)+(20/50)(19/49)=25/49≈0.510, so difference about 0.01. At the start, 13/25=0.52 and 2/5=0.4, difference 0.12. More marbles mean the remaining mix change less after taking one out, so the gap between both conditions become smaller.

y-m-27-01.title: If rain chance na 70% and rain no fall
y-m-27-01.topic: Wetin probability mean: rain chance and ratio from data collected many times
y-m-27-01.goal: Separate one result from probability (likelihood), judge how much to trust forecast from ratios collected over many days, and each time new data come, decide with reasons if you keep or change your judgment.
y-m-27-01.material:
Weather forecast say “tomorrow chance of rain na 70%”, but rain no fall the next day. Seojin say “forecast wrong”, and Haeun say “70% mean rain go fall for 70% of the 24 hours, around 17 hours.”
For this task, “70% chance of rain” mean “if many days get similar forecast conditions, rain fall on about 70% of dem”; one day with even small rain count as “rain day”. Think too say weather forecast fit get errors. (Read 70% as 0.7 or 7 out of 10.)
y-m-27-01.thinking.1: Separate one result from a ratio over many tries
y-m-27-01.thinking.2: Revise your judgment with new information
y-m-27-01.prereq.0: Know probability as a number wey show how likely something happen
y-m-27-01.prereq.1: Write fractions and decimals as percentages (Grade 6 elementary level)
y-m-27-01.s.s1.prompt: Information go come one piece at a time. Each time choose your thought; when next data show, decide if you go keep or change am.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.0: At every step, calculate “(rain days) ÷ (forecast days)” and put am beside forecast number.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which one show forecast accuracy: result from one day or record from many days.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.info: On the day forecast say rain chance na 70%, rain no fall.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this one result, you fit talk “forecast wrong”?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.after: 70% forecast too mean “around 30% chance no rain”. So one day of no rain no make us claim the forecast wrong. To evaluate forecast, gather many days like that and look all of dem together.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Rain no fall, so this forecast wrong
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You conclude only from the fact say rain no fall. 70% too include 30% chance of no rain.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Even with 70%, rain fit no fall, so hard to say from only one day
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You separate one result from likelihood. More data go help check this thought.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 70% mean rain continue for about 17 hours that day
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read probability as ratio of time. 70% mean more like “how many days rain likely to fall”.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Rain no fall, so real probability that day na 30%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You reverse probability after seeing the result. Even after result, likelihood when forecast made no change.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Over last year this agency forecast “70% chance of rain” for 40 days altogether, and rain fall on 28 of dem.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at this data, wetin you go do with your first thought?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.after: 28÷40=0.7, so this agency 70% forecasts match real rain ratio. The 12 days with no rain represent the 30% share, so forecast no miss. You fit keep your first thought “one day's result no enough to know”, and now add evidence from 40-day ratio too.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: All 12 days with no rain be wrong forecasts, so hard to trust forecast
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You count every no-rain day as “wrong”. With a 70% forecast, e normal for rain no fall around 3 times out of 10.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 40 days plenty, so from now on e go be right exactly 70% of the time
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 40 days na useful data to estimate, but e no guarantee the future.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 28/40=0.7, match 70%, and the 12 no-rain days no conflict with forecast
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You compare data ratio directly with forecast number. The 12 days represent 30% share.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The first thought, say one day's result no enough, remain same even after checking 40 days
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You keep your first thought. But now we get new evidence, ratio over 40 days, no be only one day; better to include that evidence in your words.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Another forecast app get rain on only 15 of 40 days this year when e forecast “70% chance of rain”.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Wetin you think about this app “70% chance of rain”?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If na 70%, we expect around 28 of 40 days get rain. 15 na 13 days less, so the app 70% no seem match real outcome. We no fit say chance get no effect at all, so watching longer reasonable too. Still, more evidence make judgment clearer.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 15/40 around 0.38, very different from 70%, so hard to trust the app 70%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You change your judgment after comparing data ratio with forecast number.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 15 of 40 days about the same as 70%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you calculate 15÷40, e no be 0.7. Compare am with 28 days.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 40 days fit be few, so allow chance and watch longer
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Na careful approach. But for 70%, expect around 28 of 40; 15 na 13 less, difference too big to count as chance.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Even if the apps different, the number still 70%, so results suppose be same
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even with same number, different forecast methods fit get different real accuracy. Check with data.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.reflect: Each time you see first day's result, 40-day record, and other app record, how your judgment change (or why e no change)? How you connect “70%” with the ratio of days rain actually fall?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.prompt: Reply Seojin “forecast wrong”. Use last year's data (28 of 40 days) as evidence, and say what extra data you need to know how much to trust the forecast.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the order to compare the two data: forecast number (70%) and ratio of days rain actually fall.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.1: Start your sentence by separating “one time” from “many times”.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You explain with your own words if one day of no rain conflict with 70% or no?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You use figures like 28 days and 40 days as evidence?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: The extra data you say you need fit really help evaluate forecast?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.model.0: We no fit call am wrong from one day's result alone. A 70% forecast mean rain fit no fall; over last year, rain fall on 28 of the 40 days forecast at 70%, matching 70%. To evaluate forecast, gather many similar days and check the rain-day ratio.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.model.1: One time no rain no enough to know. 28 of 40 days na 0.7, close to 70%. So hard to say this forecast wrong; more days of records go make us know better.

y-m-27-02.title: What be the probability say thumbtack point face up?
y-m-27-02.topic: Wetin probability mean: estimate outcome probability wey no occur equally often using relative frequency
y-m-27-02.goal: Understand say having only 2 outcomes no mean each probability na 1/2; estimate probability from different groups with different throw counts, then explain how new data go change your estimate.
y-m-27-02.material:
Dem drop thumbtack on desk and record if e land with point facing up or lying sideways. One throw get only these 2 outcomes; same thumbtack drop on same floor, and each throw no affect the next.
Records of 4 groups (group: number of throws / times point face up)
Group 1: 10 throws / 7 times
Group 2: 40 throws / 18 times
Group 3: 150 throws / 66 times
Group 4: 800 throws / 349 times
(All 4 groups together get 440 out of 1000 throws.)
y-m-27-02.thinking.0: Separate number of outcomes from probability
y-m-27-02.thinking.1: Compare evidence while considering amount of data
y-m-27-02.thinking.2: Revise an estimate with new data
y-m-27-02.prereq.0: Wetin probability mean and writing am as number from 0 to 1
y-m-27-02.prereq.1: Write (number of times outcome happen) ÷ (total number of tries) as decimal
y-m-27-02.s.s1.prompt: What be the best way to state probability say thumbtack point face up?
y-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the 4 groups, write (times facing up) ÷ (number of throws) as decimal.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare ratios for groups with few throws and those with many; wetin you notice?
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.a: Only 2 outcomes dey, so probability of facing up exactly 1/2
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.a: Having 2 outcomes different from both happening equally often. Check records: any group get facing-up ratio above half, or below?
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.b: Group 1 first throw ratio 0.7 (7/10) na the value to use as standard
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.b: Na ratio from group with only 10 throws. With few throws, chance fit have big effect. Compare am with other groups' ratios.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.c: Na 440 out of 1000, so estimate around 0.44, but value fit change
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.c: You use data with plenty throws and think say value fit change too.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.d: Around 0.44 (349/800) from Group 4 with most throws na the most trustworthy
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.d: You use only the group with most throws. E reasonable because close to combined value. Good to think too if any reason dey to ignore other groups.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.e: Thumbtack shape uneven, so hard to even talk about probability
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.e: When you throw many times under same conditions, the ratio gather around some value. Compare the groups' ratios.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.explain: 440 out of 1000 mean estimate around 0.44; this judgment use the widest data. Group 4 alone na 0.436 (349÷800), almost same. Group 1's 0.7, Group 2's 0.45, Group 3's 0.44, and Group 4's 0.436 show the ratio gathering around 0.44 as throws increase. This no be fixed true value but estimate, so e fit change small if we throw more.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.acc.0: Using Group 4 ratio, about 0.436, because e get most throws also reasonable. E almost same as combined 0.44.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.prompt: A fifth group drop same thumbtack on same floor 20 times and point face up 6 times (0.3). Jihu talk, “0.3 come out, so 0.44 na wrong value.” Write your view with evidence.

y-m-27-05.prereq.0: Wetin probability mean and writing am as number from 0 to 1
y-m-27-05.title: If you throw dice 6 times, a 6 must come out?
y-m-27-05.topic: Calculate probability: can we find chance of “at least once” by adding?
y-m-27-05.goal: Make counterexamples yourself to show when the rule “add one-throw probability as many times as number of throws” no work, and correct probability for 2 throws by listing all cases.
y-m-27-05.material: When rolling one fair die many times, Hayun make rule about chance of getting 6 at least once. “Chance of 6 on one throw na 1/6. So chance of getting 6 at least once in n throws na 1/6 added n times, which na n/6.” (Die fair, and throws no affect each other.)
y-m-27-05.thinking.0: Make example (counterexample) where rule no work
y-m-27-05.thinking.2: Use the range a probability must stay inside
y-m-27-05.prereq.1: Experience listing the 36 results of throwing two dice as (first number, second number)
y-m-27-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Hayun story wey hard to accept. (E fit be wrong process or wrong conclusion from am.)
y-m-27-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write results of 2 throws as (first, second), and check which cases include (6, 6).
y-m-27-05.s.s1.hint.1: With Hayun rule, calculate value as number of throws increase, like 6, 7, 8.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.0: Chance of getting 6 on one die throw na 1/6.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.1: Chance of getting 6 at least once in 2 throws na 1/6+1/6=1/3.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.2: Same way, with 6 throws na 6/6=1, so 6 must come at least once.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.3: So e impossible to get no 6 in 6 throws.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.explain: Line 1 correct. Problem start at line 2. Case (6, 6) in two throws dey both in “first throw na 6” and “second throw na 6”; adding 1/6+1/6 count am twice. Because that, line 3 “with 6 throws probability 1” and line 4 “no 6 impossible” wrong too. In fact, with 6 throws a 6 might not come out.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different throw counts n where probability under Hayun rule become strange. (n na natural number from 7 to 20.)
y-m-27-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think what range n/6 must pass before e no fit be probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put in n one by one, like 7, 8, 9, and calculate n/6.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Enter n as natural number from 7 to 20.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The n/6 from the rule greater than 1, so e no fit be probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.fail.c2: For this n, n/6 no pass 1. From which n go n/6 become strange for probability?
y-m-27-05.s.s2.explain: Probability no fit pass 1. With 7 throws, rule give 7/6; with 10 throws, 10/6, both pass 1. Since the rule sometimes give a value we no fit use as probability, Hayun rule no always work. At n=6, e give 1, but that too different from the real probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.prompt: What be chance of getting 6 at least once in 2 throws? Count the 36 results yourself to check.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write two-die results as (first, second) and draw 36 cases in table.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.hint.1: In that table, count cells wey include at least one 6.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.a: Na value Hayun find. Check among 36 cases if (6, 6) counted twice.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.b: Na value from counting 36 results yourself, counting overlap only once.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.c: Na probability of no 6. We need find case where at least one come.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.d: Na value counting only (6, 6). There also cases where only first throw na 6 or only second throw na 6.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.explain: Among 36 outcomes, 6 outcomes are (6,1) to (6,6), and 5 are (1,6) to (5,6): 11 altogether. Probability na 11/36, less than 1/3=12/36. No-6 cases na 5×5=25, so 36-25=11 same answer. The number 6 appears in those cases.

y-m-27-07.title: A fair bet with two dice
y-m-27-07.topic: Calculate probability: fair rule based on sum of two dice
y-m-27-07.goal: Use the different number of ways for each dice sum to judge if a rule fair, make several fair rules yourself, and check dem.
y-m-27-07.material:
Throw red die and blue die together and look at sum. Both dice fair, and all 36 outcomes (red number, blue number) equally likely. Number of ways to get each sum dey below.
Sum 2: 1 way, sum 3: 2 ways, sum 4: 3 ways, sum 5: 4 ways, sum 6: 5 ways, sum 7: 6 ways, sum 8: 5 ways, sum 9: 4 ways, sum 10: 3 ways, sum 11: 2 ways, sum 12: 1 way (36 ways altogether)
Yeonu and Seoa wan make “a bet where winner depend on the sum”. No tie; whatever the sum, one of dem win.
y-m-27-07.thinking.1: Make different rules wey meet a condition
y-m-27-07.thinking.2: Explain why e fair using number of cases
y-m-27-07.prereq.0: Experience listing 36 outcomes of two dice as (red number, blue number)
y-m-27-07.prereq.1: Experience writing probability as (number of cases) ÷ (total cases)
y-m-27-07.s.s1.prompt: First rule: “If sum na 6 or less, Yeonu win; if e 7 or more, Seoa win.” This rule fair?
y-m-27-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each sum in table, add separately the cases for sums 6 or less and sums 7 or more.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check if number of kinds of sums and number of cases be same thing.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.a: Seoa get more chance to win than Yeonu
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.a: You calculate and compare cases where sum 6 or under and where sum 7 or above.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.b: E fair. There are 5 kinds of sums against 6 kinds, quite close
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.b: Look like you only count number of sum kinds. Check table: each sum get different number of ways.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.c: Yeonu get advantage. Smaller sums come out more often
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.c: Use number of cases for each sum in table to check if smaller sums come out more.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.d: We no know until we throw dice
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.d: The number of cases already fixed, so we fit compare likelihood without throwing.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.explain: Sums 6 or less get 1+2+3+4+5=15 cases, and sums 7 or more get 6+5+4+3+2+1=21 cases. Yeonu chance na 15/36, Seoa na 21/36, so Seoa get advantage.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose 4 different sums for Yeonu to win (Seoa win on the rest), then make and enter 3 different fair rules where both get exactly same chance. Each sum na integer from 2 to 12. (Sums a, b, c, d.)
y-m-27-07.s.s2.hint.0: Find number of cases for each sum in table and look for 4 numbers whose total na 18.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.hint.1: Put the sum with most cases first, then make the other 3 sums bring total to 18.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.ok.c1: All 4 sums na integers from 2 to 12.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Sums must be integers from 2 to 12.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Cases where Yeonu wins must be exactly 18 of 36.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Yeonu cases no total 18. Check table cases for each sum and add dem.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.explain: Number of ways to get sum x na 6−|x−7|. If 4 sums give total 18 cases, Yeonu and Seoa each get 18 of 36, so fair. Just changing order of the same 4 sums still counts the same rule.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one rule you make and explain why e fair, using number of cases.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write each of your 4 sums beside its case count and add them.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write too the total cases for remaining sums Yeonu no win on.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You write the 4 sums in your chosen rule and how many cases each get?
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You say 18 of 36 cases go to Yeonu and other 18 go to Seoa?
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.model.0: The sums 3, 6, 7, 8 where Yeonu wins get 2+5+6+5=18 cases. Half of 36; Seoa get other 18, so same chance and fair.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.model.1: If sums na 4, 5, 7, 8, cases na 3+4+6+5=18, half of 36. Seoa too get 18, so both same chance and fair.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.prompt: Which of these rules give Yeonu and Seoa same chance of winning?
y-m-27-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each rule, find and add the table case counts for sums Yeonu win on.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare if the sum na half of 36, that is 18.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.a: Yeonu win when sum na multiple of 5; Seoa win for all other sums
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.a: Multiples of 5 na 5 and 10. Add their table case counts and compare with half of 36.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.b: Yeonu win when sum 8 or more; Seoa win when 7 or less
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.b: Add and compare case counts for sums 8 or more and sums 7 or less.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.c: Yeonu win when both dice show same number; Seoa win when different
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.c: Count results with same numbers, from (1,1) to (6,6), and compare with 36 cases.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.d: Yeonu win when sum even; Seoa win when sum odd
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.d: Add cases for even sums and odd sums separately and compare with half of 36.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.explain: Even sums get 1+3+5+5+3+1=18 cases; odd sums get 2+4+6+4+2=18, equal. Multiples of 5 (sums 5, 10) get only 4+3=7, far below half of 36; 8 or more get 5+4+3+2+1=15, less than 7 or below (21); same dice numbers have 6 cases, far less than 30 with different numbers.

y-m-27-08.title: How much a best-of-three help the stronger side?
y-m-27-08.topic: Calculate probability: compare best-of-three with one game when single-game win rate same
y-m-27-08.goal: Predict if winning chance change with match format (one game, best-of-three) when one-game win rate same; find missing case in calculation and correct it, then check if prediction hold when both have equal win rates.
y-m-27-08.material:
Mina and Taeo play board game. In one game, Mina win chance na 0.6, Taeo na 0.4, and no tie. One game's result no affect others, and each game use same win rate.
Both talk, “Should we decide with one game or best-of-three (first to win 2 games)?”
y-m-27-08.thinking.1: Find missing case in a solution
y-m-27-08.thinking.2: Change condition to check your judgment
y-m-27-08.prereq.0: Experience finding chance of independent events happening one after another
y-m-27-08.prereq.1: Experience finding chance when something fit happen in different ways
y-m-27-08.s.s1.prompt: Compared with 0.6 chance in one-game match, wetin you think Mina chance to win best-of-three go be? Predict before calculating.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare cases where Taeo wins one game with cases where Taeo wins a three-game match.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine cases where Mina win under 2 games.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.a: E bigger than 0.6. More games make skill show
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.a: Na idea say when games increase, chance effect reduce. Good prediction to check by calculation.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.b: E smaller than 0.6. She need win 2 games, harder
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.b: You only look at Mina needing more wins. Think too say Taeo too must win 2.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.c: E same as 0.6. One-game win rate same, so same
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.c: You focus on one-game win rate. Think how one lucky result affect full match when game count increase.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.d: We no fit know from one-game win rate alone
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.d: One-game rate given and same for each game, so we fit calculate when match format change.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.explain: This prediction na before-calculation judgment. Check the solution below and calculate if prediction correct.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.prompt: Seoyeon calculate Mina chance to win best-of-three like this. Choose the line hard to believe. (It fit be wrong process or wrong conclusion.)
y-m-27-08.s.s2.hint.0: List in order of wins and losses all cases where Mina win third game and result become 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find probability of every case you list and count how many Seoyeon miss.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.0: One game, Mina win chance 0.6, lose chance 0.4, and games no affect each other.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.1: For Mina to win 2:0, she must win first 2 games, so chance na 0.6×0.6=0.36.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.2: For Mina to win 2:1, only one order dey (win, lose, win), so chance na 0.6×0.4×0.6=0.144.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.3: So Mina chance to win best-of-three na 0.36+0.144=0.504.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.4: 0.504 less than 0.6 for one-game, so best-of-three disadvantage Mina.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.explain: Lines 1 and 2 correct. Problem na line 3. For Mina to win 2:1, she fit lose one of first two games in 2 ways: (win, lose, win) or (lose, win, win). So chance of 2:1 na 0.6×0.4×0.6×2=0.288. Therefore line 4 sum suppose 0.36+0.288=0.648, and line 5 conclusion wrong too.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.prompt: What be chance Mina win best-of-three?
y-m-27-08.s.s3.hint.0: Split the match ending into 2:0 and 2:1 and find each probability.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check how many orders of wins and losses make 2:1, and the probability each order multiply.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.a: Na value from Seoyeon wrong solution. Check if you find all orders wey make 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.b: Na value adding 2:0 case and both orders wey make 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.c: Na value counting only 2:0 wins. There also cases where she reach game 3 and win.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.d: Look like doubling 0.36 chance of 2:0. The 2:1 cases get different values.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.explain: 2:0 na 0.6×0.6=0.36; 2:1 get 2 orders, so 2×0.6×0.4×0.6=0.288; total 0.648. First prediction (bigger than 0.6) correct. If you play all 3 games and count cases where she win 2 or more, same result.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.prompt: Now if chance Mina and Taeo win one game both na 0.5, what be Mina chance to win best-of-three?
y-m-27-08.s.s4.hint.0: Check if problem change when you swap Mina and Taeo places.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.hint.1: Calculate chances for 2:0 and 2:1 separately and add dem.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.a: E bigger than 0.5. More games give Mina advantage
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.a: Before, side with higher one-game win rate get advantage. Check if any reason one side get advantage when both rates same.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.b: E less than 0.5. She must win 2 games, so more disadvantage
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.b: Taeo too must win 2 games. Compare if their situations same.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.c: We no fit know if e bigger or smaller than 0.5 without calculating
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.c: We fit calculate. But since both conditions exactly same, symmetry fit tell us too.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.d: Exactly 0.5. More games no give either side advantage
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.d: You use the fact say swapping same conditions make no difference. Calculation 0.25+2×0.125=0.5 too.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.explain: If one-game win rate same, 2:0 na 0.5×0.5=0.25; 2:1 na 2×0.5×0.5×0.5=0.25; total 0.5. Both get same conditions, so chance either one win same. More games favor “the side with higher one-game win rate”; game count itself no favor either side.
